sweep_summary: Three target items for Mundari (mund1320; catalog classification conflict between Hoffmann 1903 initial, Cook 1965 closed-final-attracts, Sinha 1975, Osada 1992/2008, and the Horo/Anderson instrumental line). Two were obtained and read in full as open author copies recovered through Internet Archive copy of Donegan's University of Hawaii 'Papers' directory (the live ling.hawaii.edu paths now 404): Donegan 1993 (LTBA 16(1):1-43; also two SEAlang scans, one scanned) and Donegan & Stampe 2004 (YSALL 2004:3-36; publisher DOI 10.1515/9783110179897.3 closed). Both are family-level typological essays: Munda word accent is 'falling'/initial, with light+heavy disyllables accenting the heavy second syllable and longer words keeping the accent on the second syllable from the left; Sora is the exemplar and Mundari is never given an accent statement, so they refine the reading of the catalog conflict (Hoffmann and Cook become two faces of one weight-conditioned left-edge rule) without deciding Mundari's coding. Anderson 2020 (Brill, ch.6 pp.157-197, doi 10.1163/9789004425606_008) is paywalled (Brill bot-wall, Unpaywall closed, no PAR/Living Tongues copy); only its abstract was read via an Internet Archive copy, and it is silent on Mundari word stress; priority medium (Harvard e-access). An extra open item, Donegan & Stampe 2002 (BLS 28S:111-120), was downloaded and is silent on Mundari accent. No first-hand Mundari stress statement was found; the catalog's deciding sources are not superseded. all lookups were done by direct download (Crossref, Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar API, the Internet Archive).

new_statements.quote: Although Munda accent is word-initial, in iambic words, i.e. words in which a light (open) initial syllable precedes a heavy (closed or long-voweled) second syllable, most Munda languages treat the light initial syllable as an anacrusis or pickup syllable, and put the heavy second syllable on the accent, as in Sora ebɔy 'one'. Disyllabic words of iambic shape thus have accent on the final syllable. In Munda such words are common enough that some observers, noting this final accent but not investigating what kind of rule puts it there, have concluded that Munda languages have final accent. But if additional syllables are added to such words in Munda, the accent stays on the second syllable from the beginning of the word.

new_statements.reading: A family-level (Munda) rule, illustrated with Sora and not with Mundari data: word accent is initial, except that a light initial syllable before a heavy (closed/long) second syllable is treated as an anacrusis and the heavy second syllable is accented; in longer words the accent stays on the second syllable from the left rather than tracking the word end; balanced LL/HH words are initial-accented. Read against the catalog's conflict record it makes Hoffmann 1903 (generally initial) and Cook 1965 (final if closed, else penult, in disyllables) two faces of one left-edge, weight-conditioned rule, and it agrees with the carried Osada 2008/Sinha 1975 reports that trisyllables are never initial. It is impressionistic and not first-hand for Mundari, so it cannot decide the Mundari coding; the held Horo et al. 2023/2025 instrumental studies (no robust word-level prominence cue) remain the most direct Mundari evidence.

While duration appears to correlate well with phrasal or utterance boundaries, none of these three acoustic cues showed statistically significant patterns in signaling prominence. ... these segmental cues [mid-vowel height, onset duration] may correlate better as signals of prominence in Mundari. sources.note: Newest instrumental study (10 speakers recorded, 4 analysed; 400 disyllables + 200 monosyllables): no statistically significant duration/intensity/F0 cue of word prominence, weak iambic segmental cues, argues Mundari lacks a phonological-word level; our record stops at the 2023 TAI paper and should cite this as the current state of the instrumental line.

sources.quote: p.86: 'In case of word level prosody, to date no acoustic cue seems to characterize or define the unit of phonological word. Instead, duration seems to mark the right edge of utterances, not words. sources.quote: Abstract: 'This overview of Munda language history puts forth a new hypothesis of how the original Austroasiatic typology of prosody and morphosyntax came to fit into the current Munda morphosyntactic template via revised notions of changes in prosody and morphotactics. In addition, it takes the view that Munda languages are Austroasiatic languages that moved west from MSEA and that Munda has more typological similarity to MSEA AA languages than previously supposed.'

sources.note: Only the abstract was reachable. It announces a diachronic account of Munda prosody at the proto-Munda level ('revised notions of changes in prosody and morphotactics') and says nothing specific about where word stress falls in Mundari. Given that Anderson is the co-author of the held Mundari instrumental papers (Horo & Anderson 2021; Horo, Gogoi & Anderson 2023; Horo, Anderson & Gogoi 2025), the chapter may contain a comparative survey of Kherwarian/Mundari prominence, but that cannot be confirmed from the abstract.
